question: Half of Greece’s population (5 241 300 individuals) lives in 4.3% of the country's territory. This is particularly detrimental to the quality of life, because of both climate conditions and the lack of urban planning. In 2021, over 80% of the population lived in just 277 of the 6 138 municipalities, i.e.4.5% of the total.

Naturally, increased crime and mental health, traffic and housing problems are associated with uncontrolled urbanisation of this kind. The absence of a regional development model and the pressure for ‘social progress’ have led to urbanisation. The excessively unequal distribution of the population decreases development prospects for the provinces and puts a strain on the demographic situation.

The pressurised nature of life in the capital reduces the opportunities for enjoying a safe and highquality family life. The solution lies in redistributing the population, through a national strategy for the sustainable development of the regions.

The expansion of tourism, technological and industrial investment, the provision of digital services, remote working and the provision of adequate healthcare structures will act as catalysts for decentralisation. In the light of the above: 1.
How is a successful national plan for regional development evaluated and rewarded?
What tools could the Greek regions and municipalities use to attract residents from Attica?
What decision-making tools could help the Greek local authorities to make decisions that will be successful in rendering them more attractive to investment, and to residents/workers?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.3.2024) 1. The Partnership Agreement1 is the strategic instrument for planning and implementation of structural funds in Greece. It includes an integrated approach to address demographic challenges of regions.

Its investment strategy is supporting policies increasing employment, particularly for young people, and addressing brain drain, equal participation of women in employment, access to health and childcare services, and measures to address the country’s demographic trends. Resources are earmarked to increase territorial cohesion through integrated policies.

In 20212027 funding allocated to regional programmes increased from EUR 5.9 to 8.1 billion. 2. Approximately 78% of the total European Regional Development Fund allocations (EUR 10.6 billion) are invested in the less developed regions, and all of the Just Transition Fund allocation (EUR 1.6 billion) will be spent outside of Attica.
This will much improve accessibility, digital connectivity and network coverage of mountainous regions and remote islands, health and social services, water and wastewater networks2. 3.

The Commission’s Communication on Harnessing talent in Europe’s regions introduced the Talent Booster Mechanism, an initiative to support EU regions affected by accelerated decline of their working age population and to train, retain and attract people, skills and competences needed to address the impact of demographic transition.

Furthermore, the EU Regional Competitiveness Index3 measures the competitiveness for NUTS-2 (Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics)4 level regions in the EU, and their ability to offer an attractive environment for firms and residents, providing a valuable tool for decision makers.

1 Adopted by the Commission in June 2021. 2 All interventions that contribute to quality of life and the attractiveness of regions outside Attica. 3 https://ec.europa.eu/regional_policy/information-sources/maps/regional-competitiveness_en 4 Nomenclature of territorial units for statistics (https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/nuts/overview).
